title: Wire-safe TACO
description: The subset of a bitwrench TACO that is safe to accept from something you do not trust — a device posting to triops, a model generating UI, a server streaming it. Deliberately smaller than a full TACO: it describes structure only, never behaviour. The `o` block (state, render, lifecycle hooks, handles) and every `on*` attribute are excluded, because both carry executable code and neither is serialisable. What is left is exactly the part that can travel over a wire, which is why the schema-able subset and the trust-boundary subset turn out to be the same subset. triops validates against this when allow_taco_render is enabled; see docs/api.md.

t.description: Tag name. Restricted to elements that cannot execute or load code — no script, iframe, object, embed, link, style, meta, base, form.

a.description: Attributes. propertyNames blocks every on* handler by pattern rather than by list, so a new event name cannot slip through, and names three more by hand: srcdoc and formaction execute, and style is a defacement vector — a fixed, full-viewport node covering the page it was meant to be a card inside. Interactivity travels as a NAME, not a function: `action: "restart-pump"` (or the class bw_act_restart-pump that bitwrench's action param emits) means the client dispatches through a registry it already owns. The sender proposes intent; the receiver decides what intent does, and can refuse. That is what lets a button cross a trust boundary when a handler never could.

c.description: Content: text, one node, or an array of either. Recursion is what makes this worth having as a schema rather than a checklist.

safeUrl.description: Relative, http, https, or mailto — an allowlist, so blob:, filesystem: and whatever ships next are excluded without needing to be named. Leading whitespace is rejected outright: browsers trim it before resolving the scheme, so ' javascript:...' is a URL that looks relative to a naive check and is not one to the browser.
